sections.text: A web server is a program that reads text from a client and writes text back. The text follows a set of rules called HTTP. In this lesson we write the brain of a tiny server using only pure functions: they take a String in and give a String out, with no network involved. That makes them easy to write and easy to test. In the next lesson we plug them into a real network connection.

An HTTP request is plain text. The first line (the request line) has the method, the path and the version. Then come header lines like Name: value. A blank line ends the headers, and anything after it is the body. Lines end with \r\n (carriage return, line feed), written "\r\n" in a Rust string.
split_once cuts a string at the first match and gives back the two halves as a tuple, wrapped in an Option (None if the text was not found). We use it a lot below.

Now the full program, in three steps. (1) parse_request turns the raw text into a Request struct, or a ParseError if the text is broken. Header names are lowercased because HTTP header names are not case sensitive. (2) route looks at the method and path and decides what to answer. (3) Response::to_text builds the reply text: a status line, headers, a blank line and the body. Content-Length must be the body's length in bytes, which is what len() gives.

The match in route looks at the method and the path together, as a tuple, just like the commands in the text adventure. The last arm answers 404 Not Found for everything else. handle ties it together: broken input becomes a 400 Bad Request instead of a crash. Nothing here touches the network, so you can try any request text you like.

The status code is a number the client reads: 200 means success, 404 means the thing was not found, 400 means the client sent something broken, and 500 means the server itself failed. Browsers show these as pages like "404 Not Found".

This is the shape of most web frameworks: parse bytes into a typed request, route on (method, path), return a typed response. Frameworks like axum, actix-web and rocket do the same with extractors and macros. A real parser must also handle HTTP/1.1 details this toy skips: header values that continue over several lines, chunked bodies, Content-Length checks, and limits on request size. Parsing untrusted input with Result instead of panicking is what keeps a server alive.

exercise.prompt: The tiny server in route() only knows the home page. Add an About page: a request for the path /about should answer with status 200 and the body About us, while other unknown paths still give 404. The program should print three lines: 200 Home page, 200 About us, 404 Not found. Hint: add the match arm "/about" => (200, "About us") before the _ arm.
exercise.expectedOutput:
200 Home page
200 About us
404 Not found

quiz.question: What separates the headers of an HTTP request from its body?
options: A semicolon on a line of its own after the last header
A blank line, written \r\n\r\n after the last header
The word BODY followed by a colon at the start of a line

quiz.question: What does the server answer when no route matches?
options: A 404 Not Found response, from the last match arm
A 200 OK response that has an empty body
A panic, because a match must name every possible path

quiz.question: Why are parse_request, route and handle easy to test?
options: They use unsafe code that the compiler has already checked for you
They need a running network connection before they can be called even once
They are pure functions: text in, text out, with no network involved
